meta.title: Who really said "Blind belief in authority is the greatest enemy of truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Einstein — a letter to Jost Winteler, 8 July 1901, written at 22 after a journal editor brushed him off. The German is 'Autoritätsdusel', a word with no clean English equivalent, so every English version is a translator's choice.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Blind belief in authority is the greatest enemy of truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Real: Einstein to Jost Winteler, 8 July 1901, aged 22. But the key German word — Autoritätsdusel — is untranslatable, so there is no canonical English wording.

answer.label: Verified — but the English is a translator's choice
answer.sourceLine: Genuine. Einstein wrote it on 8 July 1901, aged twenty-two, in a letter to Jost Winteler — his former boarding-house host in Aarau — after the editor of Annalen der Physik dismissed his criticisms out of hand. The German is ‘Autoritätsdusel ist der grösste Feind der Wahrheit’. The catch: Autoritätsdusel is an archaic colloquialism with no clean English equivalent, so every English version you have seen is a translator’s decision, not Einstein’s words.

source.excerpt: Autoritätsdusel ist der grösste Feind der Wahrheit.
trail: The letter is catalogued in the scholarly edition of Einstein’s papers as Volume 1, Document 115, and is quoted in the biography The Private Lives of Albert Einstein (1993). The recipient, Jost Winteler, had housed Einstein as a schoolboy in Aarau Wikiquote, sourced ↗.

The occasion is small and human: Paul Drude, editing Annalen der Physik, had brushed aside the young Einstein’s objections to his electron theory of metals. The line is written in irritation, not as a philosophical maxim.

An attempt to debunk the English wording as a fabrication was withdrawn by its own author, who concluded he had been wrong to call the line fake and added that he was no longer sure which English rendering is best. German speakers and an Einstein Papers translator in the thread proposed different wordings — from ‘unthinking acceptance of authority’ to ‘authority gone to one’s head’ — so what was settled was that the letter is real, not that any one English version is definitive the retracted debunk ↗.
source.excerptNote: Einstein’s German. Dusel means something like a daze or befuddlement, so Autoritätsdusel is roughly ‘authority-daze’ — being punch-drunk on authority. English has no single word for it, which is why the translations diverge so widely; the Einstein Papers Project’s own published rendering is ‘authority gone to one’s head is the greatest enemy of truth.’

source.rightsNote: Mixed, and worth reading before reuse. The German original has been public domain in the UK and EU since 1 January 2026 (Einstein died in 1955); its US status depends on first publication in the scholarly edition and is unresolved. Separately, any specific published English translation carries its own copyright — the scholarly edition’s translation volumes and the 1993 biography’s rendering are each protected. The safest practice, and the one we follow here, is to quote the German and cite the document number, adding a plain gloss of your own rather than lifting a named translator’s sentence. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity and was awarded the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics (presented in 1922). This line comes from long before any of that: he was twenty-two, unemployed, recently graduated and unable to get an academic post, and had just been patronised by a journal editor. The scepticism toward authority it expresses was not a late elder-statesman pose — it was there at the very beginning, and it was personal.

misattribution.heading: What to watch for
misattribution.intro: The attribution is solid — a dated letter with a scholarly document number. The difficulty is entirely linguistic, and it is the reason this quote keeps getting accused of being fake.

items.why: ‘Blind belief in authority,’ ‘blind obedience to authority,’ ‘unthinking respect for authority’ and ‘a foolish faith in authority’ are all in circulation — and the Einstein Papers Project’s own published translation renders it ‘authority gone to one’s head is the greatest enemy of truth.’ Even that, the nearest thing to an official version, is one choice among several: he wrote one German noun, and English has no equivalent.

The popular English was once flagged as an invention. The author of that debunking later withdrew it himself, concluding he had been wrong to call the line fake — while adding that he remained unsure which English rendering is best. The letter is real; only the English wording is negotiable the thread ↗.
Quoted today as a grand statement about science and dogma. Written as a private complaint about a journal editor who would not engage with his criticism.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Einstein, in a letter to Jost Winteler of 8 July 1901 — but he wrote Autoritätsdusel, and no English word carries it, so treat the familiar sentence as a good translation rather than his exact words the German ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the founding sentiment of the scientific temperament, delivered by the person most often invoked as an authority — which gives it a pleasing recursive edge whenever someone quotes it to win an argument.

What makes it better than its reputation is how petty the occasion was. A twenty-two-year-old with no job and no position writes to an old family friend to complain that an editor would not take his criticism seriously, and produces a line that outlives the editor, the journal issue, and the argument.
context.detailsSummary: The word that will not translate
detailsBody: Dusel in German means a daze, a stupor, a befuddled state — also, colloquially, dumb luck.
Autoritätsdusel is therefore closer to ‘authority-daze’: not belief in authority, but being punch-drunk on it.
‘Blind belief’ catches the blindness but loses the stupor; ‘unthinking respect’ catches the thoughtlessness but sounds far too polite.
Because no rendering is definitive, quoting the German and citing document 115 is both the most accurate and the safest option.
context.pull: He wrote one German noun. English needs a whole phrase, and still misses it.
